topics: 🔥 A Sleeping Watchman's Punishment — struck with a staff, his garment burned
💬 The Value of Rebuke — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's guiding principle for life
🏃 From Footrace to Lottery — how a broken leg changed the ash-removal procedure forever
🚪 The Pre-Dawn Procession — opening the wicket, splitting into two groups, checking every vessel
🔥 Removing the Ashes in Total Darkness — guided only by the glow of the altar fire and the sound of a hidden mechanism

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Discipline, Reform, and the First Rite of the Day
overview.subtitle: Tamid 28a–28b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by completing the account of the officer who patrolled the night watches — a sleeping watchman was struck and had his garment burned, a harsh but instructive precedent the Gemara uses to launch into teachings about the value of loving rebuke. The Gemara then resolves an apparent contradiction in the ash-removal mishna by tracing its history: originally a footrace up the ramp determined who removed the ashes, until an injury led the Sages to institute a lottery instead. A new mishna details the pre-dawn procession through the Temple courtyard — two groups checking every vessel was in place — before describing, in vivid sensory detail, how the winning priest performed the ash-removal rite entirely in darkness and silence, guided only by the glow of the altar's fire and the sound of a hidden mechanism.

slides.title: 🔥 Discipline for a Sleeping Watchman, and a Lesson in Rebuke
slides.subtitle: From harsh enforcement to a broader teaching about tochacha

steps.content: 1️⃣ The officer overseeing the watches greets each guard with 'peace be upon you' — if there's no reply, the guard is asleep
2️⃣ He strikes the sleeping watchman with his staff and has license to burn his garment as discipline
3️⃣ Others hearing the commotion would say: 'That's the sound of a Levite being flogged, his clothes burned, for sleeping on watch'
4️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan's reflection: 'Praiseworthy were the early generations, who enforced judgment even for sleep beyond one's control — how much more so for deliberate wrongdoing'

5️⃣ Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's broader teaching: the right path in life is to LOVE admonition, since rebuke brings pleasantness, goodness, and blessing into the world (Proverbs 24:25); Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani adds that one who rebukes another for Heaven's sake merits closeness to God Himself

slides.title: 🏃 Resolving a Contradiction: Race, Then Lottery
slides.subtitle: Why the mishna seems to describe two different systems

nodes.content: ❓ The mishna first says whoever is READY (immersed) can remove the ashes — implying no lottery — then says the officer calls for a LOTTERY. Which is it?
🔧 Abaye's resolution: the mishna describes TWO ERAS — 'ready first' describes the OLD system (before a reform); the lottery describes the NEW system (after the reform)
🔄 Rava's alternative: BOTH clauses describe the post-reform era — 'rises early and immerses' means simply becoming ELIGIBLE to enter the lottery, not automatically winning the task

callout.label: What was the old system?
callout.text: Originally (per a parallel mishna in Yoma), any priest wanting the honor would RACE up the ramp — whoever reached within four cubits of the top first, won. If two tied, they'd raise one or two fingers for a random count (never the thumb, to prevent cheating).

slides.title: 🏃 The Incident That Changed Everything
slides.subtitle: From competitive footrace to a calm lottery
rows: Priests raced up the ramp; first to reach within four cubits of the top won the ash-removal privilege
Two tied priests would extend one or two fingers for a random count (never a thumb, to prevent manipulation)
Two priests running neck-and-neck up the ramp — one shoved the other, who fell and broke his leg
The court, seeing the danger this competition created, instituted that ash-removal would be determined ONLY by a calm lottery from then on

slides.title: 🚪 New Mishna: The Pre-Dawn Procession
slides.subtitle: Splitting into two groups to check every service vessel
slides.label: The scene:
slides.text: Near dawn, the appointed priest took a key hidden beneath a floor tablet, opened the wicket gate, and led the priestly family into the courtyard, torches lighting the way. They split into two groups — one walking the eastern portico, one the western — inspecting every service vessel along the route until both groups converged at the Chamber of the Griddle-Cake Preparer. There they declared to each other: 'Peace, all is well' — confirming every vessel was in place — before setting that day's griddle-cake preparer to begin his work. (The Gemara clarifies these porticoes were built of STONE, not wood, since Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids any tree or wooden structure beside the altar.)

slides.title: 🔥 Removing the Ashes — Alone, in the Dark
slides.subtitle: A rite performed by sound and firelight alone

steps.content: 1️⃣ No one accompanied the winning priest, and he carried no lamp — he walked only by the glow of the still-burning wood arrangement on the altar
2️⃣ The other priests couldn't see or hear him — the altar itself blocked their view

3️⃣ They knew he'd reached the right moment only when they heard the creak of ben Katin's pulley MECHANISM, raising the Basin that had been sunk in flowing water overnight (so its water wouldn't be disqualified) — 'The time has come!'
4️⃣ He sanctified his hands and feet, took the silver coal pan, ascended the altar, cleared the outer coals aside, and scooped the fully-consumed inner coals into the pan
5️⃣ He descended, turned north, walked along the ramp's east side, and heaped the coals on the floor — the same spot used for bird-offering remains and other Temple ashes

callout.label: Then the brethren joined in:
callout.text: Once the other priests saw him descend, they rushed to sanctify their own hands and feet, grabbed shovels and forks, and ascended to clear unburned limbs and fats to the altar's sides, then heaped remaining ash onto the great central mound (תַּפּוּחַ) — sometimes holding as much as 300 kor, left untouched on Festivals as a mark of the altar's honor.

summary.principle: The Temple's morning rites combined strict discipline (a sleeping watchman disciplined without exception), thoughtful reform (a dangerous footrace replaced by a peaceful lottery after an injury), and precise, almost silent choreography — a rite performed by firelight and sound alone, before the courtyard fully woke to prepare the altar for the day's offerings.

flowSteps.content: 🔥 A sleeping watchman is struck and disciplined — sparking teachings on the value of loving rebuke
🏃 An injury during a competitive footrace up the ramp leads the court to institute a calm lottery instead
🚪 Pre-dawn: two groups check every vessel, converging with 'all is well' at the griddle-cake chamber

columns.content: 🔥 The winning priest removes ashes alone, guided only by firelight and a mechanism's sound
🧹 His brethren then join to clear remaining limbs and tend the great ash heap

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: even the Temple's most routine daily task was governed by precise choreography born from real experience — including a painful lesson that led to lasting reform

quiz.q: What discipline could the officer overseeing the night watches impose on a watchman found sleeping on duty?
o: A verbal warning only
Striking him with a staff and burning his garment
Immediate expulsion from the priesthood
A monetary fine
quiz.e: The mishna describes that a sleeping watchman would be struck with the officer's staff, who also had license to burn the watchman's garment as discipline.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, how does the mishna's apparent contradiction — between 'whoever is ready removes the ashes' and 'a lottery determines who removes the ashes' — get resolved?
o: The mishna is simply an error
The two clauses describe two different historical eras: one before a reform, and one after the reform was enacted
Both clauses always applied simultaneously with no distinction
The lottery only applied on Shabbat
quiz.e: Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the mishna's clauses describe the procedure before and after the Sages instituted the lottery reform.

quiz.q: What incident led the Sages to institute a lottery for ash-removal instead of the original system?
o: A priest was late and missed his turn
Two priests racing up the ramp to reach the top first, with one shoving the other, causing a broken leg
A fire broke out on the altar
The ramp collapsed
quiz.e: The mishna in Yoma describes how a dangerous shove during a competitive race up the ramp resulted in a broken leg, prompting the court to replace the race with a safer lottery system.

quiz.q: How did the other priests know when the ash-removing priest had reached the moment to sanctify his hands and feet, since they could neither see nor hear him?
o: A bell was rung
They heard the sound of ben Katin's pulley mechanism raising the Basin that had been sunk in water overnight
Someone shouted from the altar
They simply waited a fixed amount of time
quiz.e: The mishna describes that the priests were alerted by the distinctive creaking sound of ben Katin's mechanical device raising the ritual Basin from the water where it had been kept overnight.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, why were the porticoes in the Temple courtyard permitted despite a verse prohibiting wooden structures beside the altar?
o: The verse's prohibition doesn't apply to the Temple courtyard
The porticoes mentioned in the mishna were built of stone, not wood — the prohibition applies specifically to wooden structures
Wood was permitted as long as it wasn't shaped like a tree
The prohibition was overridden by Temple necessity
quiz.e: Rav Ḥisda clarifies that the mishna's porticoes were made of stone construction materials, distinguishing them from the wooden structures forbidden by Deuteronomy 16:21.
